title: Reproduction and Population Control
summary: Asexual reproduction: a single parent, no gametes (bacteria, protista, lower plants and animals). Sexual reproduction: formation and fusion of gametes (fertilisation) giving a zygote. Gemmule: an asexual reproductive body of fresh water sponges, a tiny hard ball of undifferentiated cells (archaeocytes) covered by a resistant coat of chitin and spicules with a micropyle; it tides over unfavourable conditions (drying of ponds, winter) and the archaeocytes come out through the micropyle to form a new sponge. In insects sexes are usually separate; aphids reproduce parthenogenetically (all females). Cockroach: male has a pair of testes, vasa deferentia, ejaculatory duct, seminal vesicles, mushroom gland and gonapophyses; female has a pair of ovaries with ovarioles, oviducts, vagina, spermatheca (receives sperms), genital pouch and collaterial glands that form the ootheca (egg case).

Puberty is the period of maturation of sex organs and secondary sexual characters (males: deepening voice, beard, muscles; females: widening of pelvis, breasts, menstruation); adolescence is 10-19 years (WHO). Testes: extra-abdominal in the scrotum, which keeps the temperature 2-3 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature, suitable for sperm formation; each testis has coiled seminiferous tubules (sperm formation, spermatogenesis) and interstitial (Leydig) cells secreting testosterone. Epididymis stores sperms (viable but immotile); vas deferens carries sperms to the urethra; the urethra carries semen and urine; the penis is the copulatory organ. Accessory glands: seminal vesicles (nourishing fluid, 40-80 per cent of semen), prostate (alkaline fluid, activates sperms) and Cowper's glands (lubricating mucus). A sperm has a head with the acrosome (helps penetrate the egg), neck with centriole, middle piece with mitochondria and a tail (flagellum).

A pair of ovaries (produce ova, oestrogen and progesterone; oogenesis; follicle stages: primary follicle, Graafian follicle which ruptures at ovulation, leaving the corpus luteum), a pair of oviducts or Fallopian tubes (site of fertilisation; funnel-shaped infundibulum), uterus (pear-shaped; layers endometrium, myometrium and perimetrium; the embryo implants in it), vagina (birth canal) and external genitalia. Menstrual cycle (about 28 days): menstruation (days 1-4, shedding of the uterine lining); follicular phase (days 5-13; Graafian follicle matures and secretes oestrogen, which builds the endometrium); ovulation (13th-14th day; ovum released); luteal phase (corpus luteum secretes progesterone); if no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates and the lining is shed on about the 28th day. Menarche is the onset of menstruation (11-13 years) and menopause is the stoppage (45-50 years). In pregnancy menstruation and ovulation stop because progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and then the placenta.

Sperms stay viable in the female tract for 24-72 hours; fertilisation occurs in the oviduct; the zygote divides to form a morula (day 4), then a blastocyst (day 5), which implants in the uterine wall about a week after fertilisation (embryo to pregnancy). Embryo development: zygote, morula, blastocyst, implantation; foetus with human features by 6 weeks; birth after about 40 weeks. Placenta: an association between maternal and foetal tissue where oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother to the foetus and CO2 and wastes pass back; it is permeable to gases, nutrients and antibodies, does not allow most germs (HIV can pass), and secretes progesterone and hCG. Umbilical cord: blood vascular connection between the foetus and the placenta. Amnion: a sac filled with amniotic fluid that acts as a shock absorber. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes uterine contractions for childbirth; labour; the amnion bursts, the baby is expelled, the cord is tied and cut.

Lactation: secretion of milk by mammary glands, stimulated by prolactin (anterior pituitary) and ejected by oxytocin (posterior pituitary). Colostrum is the first thick yellowish milk, rich in proteins and fats and containing antibodies (IgA) which give passive immunity to the newborn; so a mother should feed the baby just after birth. Twins: fraternal (two ova fertilised by two sperms; may be of different sexes) and identical (one zygote divides into two separate embryos; same sex); Siamese twins are identical twins that fail to separate. New techniques: test tube baby (IVF: ova fertilised outside and the embryo placed in the uterus), artificial insemination (stored semen introduced at ovulation) and fertility drugs (FSH to stimulate follicles).

Terms: population density (individuals per sq km), birth rate or natality (live births per 1000 per year), death rate or mortality (deaths per 1000 per year), growth rate (birth rate minus death rate), census (official count). India's population was 23.8 crore in 1901 and 102.7 crore in 2001. Causes of growth: advances in agriculture and medicine, customs, illiteracy, economic reasons, desire for a male child, industrialisation. Problems: poor health, housing and education for the family; for the country, urbanisation and slums, pollution, pressure on food, water, minerals and energy. Population control: education, rhythm (safe period) method, condoms and diaphragms, intrauterine devices (copper T), oral pills, vasectomy and tubectomy (surgical), and medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) under medical supervision.

objective: Fill in the table: (a) Process: spermatogenesis; location? (b) Location: fallopian tube; process?
(a) Seminiferous tubules of the testis. (b) Fertilisation.

A is an association between maternal and foetal tissue. B is a tough structure which serves as the blood vascular connection between the foetus and the uterine wall. The embryo is enclosed in a sac C filled with D. Fill in the blanks (any two).
A: placenta. B: umbilical cord. C: amnion. D: amniotic fluid (shock absorber).
In a section of the ovary, identify the two structures A (large fluid-filled follicle with the ovum) and B (the yellowish body left after ovulation).
A: Graafian follicle. B: corpus luteum.
Name the glands: (a) the secretion forms the lubricant of semen (b) the secretion activates the sperms.
(a) Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands. (b) Prostate gland (and seminal vesicles).
Match: (a) Corpus luteum (b) Oxytocin (c) Colostrum with (i) progesterone (ii) childbirth (iii) first milk.
State true or false: (a) Testes are intra-abdominal. (b) Identical twins are always of the same sex.
(a) False – they are in the scrotum. (b) True.
Name the term: (a) onset of menstruation (b) permanent stoppage of menstruation.
(a) Number of live births per 1000 individuals per year. (b) Number of deaths per 1000 individuals per year.
vsa: What is a gemmule? State its importance in sponges.
A reproductive body of asexual reproduction with archaeocytes in a resistant covering; it tides over unfavourable conditions and develops into a new sponge when conditions improve.
Write the functions of the placenta (any two).
It supplies oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the foetus, removes CO2 and wastes from the foetus and secretes hormones (progesterone, hCG).
Differentiate between identical and fraternal twins (two points).
Identical twins arise from one zygote that splits and are of the same sex; fraternal twins arise from two ova fertilised by two sperms and may be of different sexes.
Mention two functions of the epididymis and the vas deferens.
The epididymis stores sperms; the vas deferens carries sperms from the epididymis to the urethra.
What is implantation? When does it occur?
Fixing of the blastocyst into the wall of the uterus, about a week after fertilisation.
State two causes of population explosion in India.
Advances in medicine (lower death rate) and illiteracy or social customs against family planning.
Name two permanent surgical methods of birth control.
Vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females.
Write the hormonal roles of FSH and LH in the female menstrual cycle.
FSH stimulates follicle growth and oestrogen secretion; LH causes ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum.
sa: Give reasons: (a) Testes are extra-abdominal. (b) In aphids, we can see only females. (c) A mother should feed her newborn baby just after birth.

(a) The scrotum keeps the temperature 2-3 degrees Celsius lower than the body, which is needed for sperm production. (b) Aphids reproduce parthenogenetically, so every generation consists of females. (c) The first milk, colostrum, contains antibodies that give passive immunity to the baby.
What is colostrum? Why is it essential for the newly born baby?
Colostrum is the first yellowish secretion of the mammary glands after childbirth, rich in proteins and containing IgA antibodies; it protects the newborn by giving passive immunity and nourishes it.
What is placenta? Give any two of its functions.

The placenta is the tissue formed by the union of maternal and foetal tissue, attached to the uterus by which the embryo is nourished. It supplies oxygen and food to the foetus, removes wastes and secretes progesterone.
Describe the events of the menstrual cycle.

Menstruation for 3-4 days; growth of the Graafian follicle with oestrogen builds the endometrium; ovulation on the 13th-14th day; the corpus luteum secretes progesterone; if there is no fertilisation, the lining is shed again at the end of 28 days.
Explain the structure of a human sperm.
Head with nucleus and acrosome that helps penetrate the egg, neck with centriole, middle piece with mitochondria for energy and a tail (flagellum) for movement.
Describe the functions of the accessory glands in males.
Seminal vesicles secrete fluid to nourish sperms; the prostate secretes an alkaline fluid that activates them; Cowper's glands secrete a lubricating fluid.
Explain test tube baby technique and artificial insemination.
In IVF ripe ova are taken out, fertilised with sperms in a dish and one embryo is put into the uterus; in artificial insemination stored semen is introduced into the woman at ovulation.
Write three methods of birth control.
Condoms and diaphragms (barrier), copper T (IUD) and oral pills (prevent ovulation).
la: Describe the male reproductive system of humans with the functions of its parts.

Testes (seminiferous tubules make sperms; Leydig cells make testosterone), epididymis (stores sperm), vas deferens, urethra, penis and accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper's glands) with functions.
Describe the female reproductive system of humans with the functions of its parts.
Ovaries produce ova and hormones, oviducts are the site of fertilisation, the uterus nourishes the embryo, the cervix and vagina are the birth canal.
Describe the development of the embryo from fertilisation to birth.
Fertilisation in the oviduct, zygote, morula on day 4, blastocyst on day 5, implantation on day 6-7, embryo at 4 weeks, foetus at 6 weeks, placenta, amnion, birth at about 40 weeks and lactation.
Explain the causes and effects of population growth and its control.

Causes: better medicine and agriculture, illiteracy, customs, economic reasons. Effects on the family and country: poor housing, health, education, pollution, resource depletion. Control: education, contraceptives, sterilisation and MTP.
